label: Real run on this Mac's Docker Compose stack, with synthetic traffic from klaxon.traffic: synthetic data, a simulated provider, no real money. One fault from klaxon.faults, pool-exhaustion, was injected on purpose. The alert was raised by klaxon.alerts from what the stack showed. Klaxon's loop ran live on it, through Claude Code on Aravind's seat, and stopped on diagnosed after 9 steps; any reply it got is a recorded response, not a simulation. It was offered one write action (rollback_deploy), as in week 4; in an evaluation run its gate only plans an action the diagnosis names: nobody is asked, and nothing runs. The diagnosis was compared with the fault's recorded cause by a rule (klaxon.grading), not by a person or a model. Code planned the action its diagnosis named (redeploy payments-api: PROVIDER_BREAKER on (unchanged), CHARGE_AMOUNT_UNIT cents (unchanged), REFUND_CONNECTION kept -> returned); in an evaluation run nobody is asked, and nothing ran. The fault's cause was removed by the harness's clearing (klaxon.faults).

case.name: pool-exhaustion
case.title: Payments fail: the payments API's database pool runs dry
case.right_answer: The fault's recorded cause: a deploy of the payments API with a connection leak (REFUND_CONNECTION=kept): reading a payment's refunds takes a connection from its database pool of 10 and never gives it back, so after about ten refunds the pool is empty, and every request waits for a connection until the pool's 5 s timeout, then fails with a 500.
case.remedy: roll the payments API back to REFUND_CONNECTION=returned: its new container starts with a full pool

fault.title: Payments fail: the payments API's database pool runs dry

expected_symptoms: the pool runs dry about 40 to 50 s after the deploy; then POST /payments takes 5 to 8 s (a worker thread, then the pool's 5 s wait) and fails with a 500: the p95 latency passes 7 s, and the 5xx share passes 70% within a minute
the payments API logs 'unhandled error' with PoolTimeout: no connection within 5 s
its health check fails too, so docker marks it unhealthy, while PostgreSQL itself is up
the traffic's clients retry and give up: many payments end with their outcome unknown, and arrivals past 64 in flight are shed
the money check passes: a payment that never got a connection was never charged, and one charged before its answer was lost is confirmed by its webhook
fault.remedy: roll the payments API back to REFUND_CONNECTION=returned: its new container starts with a full pool

diagnosis.hypothesis: The payments-api deploy at 17:26:23 (PROVIDER_BREAKER=on, CHARGE_AMOUNT_UNIT=cents, REFUND_CONNECTION=kept) exhausted its PostgreSQL connection pool. Likely cause: REFUND_CONNECTION=kept makes refund requests hold their DB connection, possibly across the provider call, instead of returning it promptly. Soon after the first refunds following the deploy, every POST /payments waits the full 5 s pool timeout, fails with psycopg_pool.PoolTimeout and returns 500, pushing p95 to 7.3 s. The provider is not the cause: calls to it stay at about 5 ms. Left open: I did not see the pre-deploy settings, so I cannot confirm REFUND_CONNECTION changed in this deploy. I did not directly see which requests hold connections; a leak in the new image or another setting would look the same. I did not run the money check, so book drift from failed requests is unknown.

evidence.shows: p95 of payments-api requests was about 0.02–0.04 s until 17:26:15, then 7.33 s at 17:27:15. The symptom is confirmed.
payments-api was redeployed at 17:26:23, under a minute before the jump, with REFUND_CONNECTION=kept and PROVIDER_BREAKER=on. All other services were last created at 17:24:57.
payments-api's calls to the provider stay fast (p95 about 5 ms), so the latency is not the provider's.
Every slow POST /payments trace lasts about 5.0 s, all starting after 17:26:40, which points to a fixed timeout.
A slow POST /payments returns 500 with error.type psycopg_pool.PoolTimeout after waiting 5 s for a DB connection and makes no provider call: the Postgres pool is exhausted.
Many PoolTimeout errors on POST /payments at 17:27, so the failure is widespread and ongoing.
Refunds took 8–15 ms before the deploy (17:25) and 5–5.3 s after it (from 17:26:43), so refund handling changed with the deploy and is tied to the pool exhaustion.

proposed_fix.summary: Roll payments-api back to the settings it ran before the 17:26:23 deploy, most likely restoring how refunds release their DB connection. This should free the pool and restore POST /payments latency. Afterwards run money_check: payments and refunds that failed with 500 during the incident may need follow-up if the provider processed them. Then fix the refund path to return its connection before calling the provider.

diagnosis.blast_radius: Only payments-api, which pauses a few seconds while its container is recreated; in-flight payment and refund requests fail and clients must retry. The rollback also reverts this deploy's other settings, PROVIDER_BREAKER and CHARGE_AMOUNT_UNIT, to earlier values. If an earlier value is wrong (for example a different amount unit) it could change how charges are sent, so check the previous settings in the deploy log before approving. Money already affected by failed requests stays as it is.
diagnosis.rollback_plan: If things get worse, redeploy payments-api with the current settings (PROVIDER_BREAKER=on, CHARGE_AMOUNT_UNIT=cents, REFUND_CONNECTION=kept, image sha256:7256281b9aaa) and investigate further. If pool exhaustion persists after the rollback, the cause is elsewhere (for example a leak in the image or more traffic); restarting payments-api frees the pool for a while.
